A hummingbird hangs dead still at one white orchid flower on a dripping limb, the whole background dissolved to mist so that nothing exists behind it.

A small translucent green tree frog sits in the standing water pooled at the centre of a stiff-leaved plant on the limb, sunk in up to its chin, only its eyes and the top of its head above the waterline.
A quetzal half-swallowed by a curtain of hanging moss, nothing visible but two very long green tail feathers dropping past a cluster of pale orchid flowers below — the bird itself is only implied.
A bright yellow snake lies coiled in one flat unhurried spiral on a soaking moss pad, the whole coil no wider than the limb it rests on is thick.
A tiny bright red-and-black frog sits on the flat of a wet leaf, and the water is still beaded in a ring around it, each bead catching what light there is.

A blue morpho butterfly rests on a dark wet limb with both wings spread wide, and because everything else in the frame is green or grey, it and one white orchid flower behind it are the only two bright things anywhere.
Twenty or more small pale butterflies work a single arching spray of orchid flowers in the wet air, so many of them that the spray bends slightly under the shifting weight.
A small green lizard lies pressed flat along the top of a limb, the same colour and almost the same texture as the moss beneath it, and only its raised head breaks the line of the moss.
A toucanet leans its whole body right out from the limb to reach a cluster of small dark berries, one foot still gripping the bark, its pale beak already closing around one berry.
A hummingbird sits for once, perched on a bare stem that is noticeably thinner than the single white orchid flower hanging beside it, perfectly still in a way hummingbirds almost never are.

A small blue-and-green tanager shakes water off its feathers mid-perch, and a loose burst of bright drops hangs in the air around it, each one lit from inside by the grey mist light beyond the canopy.
A green metallic beetle walks slowly across one wide wet leaf, its hard green shell throwing back a single bright point of light, the beetle no longer than the leaf is wide.
A gecko clings to a patch of bark so completely textured like wet moss that its whole small body reads as one raised ridge on the bark, giving it away only on the second look.
A small brown wren works along the underside of a thick limb, moving upside down from one patch of lichen to the next, its body no longer than the width of the limb is deep.

A hummingbird hovers at the very edge of the frame in front of a wall of soaking moss, its bill just touching a small pale flower that is nearly hidden in the green, so the bird reads as an intrusion into a world that did not arrange itself for it.

A dozen or more iridescent green-and-copper butterflies spiral slowly around a single hanging cluster of orchid flowers, the whole slow ring of them no wider across than the limb the cluster hangs from.

A small blue-and-green tanager perches on a branch where a wide flat orchid flower faces outward, and the flower is clearly larger than the bird's whole head, making the bird look like a visitor who has underestimated the room.
A tiny red-and-black frog moves across a broad flat leaf at an angle, heading for the leaf's shadowed edge, and the beaded water on the leaf parts in a faint trail behind its feet.
A translucent green tree frog grips the outside of a water-filled plant on the limb, pale green and pressed flat to it, its whole body no longer than the plant is wide.

A quetzal sits deep in a gap between two moss-covered limbs, its crimson breast the one warm colour in a frame otherwise built entirely from cold greens and silver mist, its long tail feathers hanging straight down past an orchid spray below.

A green lizard sits absolutely still on the side of a trunk where a cluster of pale roots has spread flat over the bark and clamped down, the lizard positioned among the roots so that for a moment it reads as part of the root structure.

A bright yellow snake is coiled on the top of a broad limb beside a long pad of dark green moss, the coil sitting exactly as neatly as something placed there, taking up no more room than the moss pad is wide.
A blue morpho butterfly drifts upward through the frame at the far edge, wings fully open, its open wings no wider than the hanging moss curtain beside it is thick.
Twenty or more small butterflies in orange and black settle and resettle on a single arching branch of small pale flowers, and from a distance the whole branch appears to be slowly breathing.

A green metallic beetle clings to the underside of a broad wet leaf at the frame's lower corner, hanging there as though it has decided the underside of things is simply the more interesting side, its shell the one hard, lacquered surface in a frame full of soft and dripping green.
